title: “The Mask is Off!” The Ortega Regime in Nicaragua Abolishes Elections. Now What?
author: Laura Carlsen
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Daniel_Ortega_on_July_20_2024-680x486.jpg)

Photograph Source: Duma.gov.ru - [CC BY
4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

Nicaragua’s co-president, Daniel Ortega finally came right out and said it:
“Forget about it—there won’t be any more elections here!”

He was speaking to a hypothetical opposition, which could not have been
present since nearly all its members have been exiled, imprisoned or forced
into hiding. The announcement came on July 19, the anniversary of the triumph
of the Sandinista Revolution. The defeat of a brutal authoritarian dictator,
celebrated around the world 47 years ago to the day, had come full circle.

I remember the exact moment we got the news that the Sandinistas had taken
Managua and the dictator, Anatasio Somoza, had fled the country. Images of the
people’s army pouring into the capital, surrounded by a euphoric population,
sent a message throughout a world that self-determination and democracy could
succeed even during the Cold War.

Years of armed struggle in Nicaragua led to that unforgettable day, aided by
U.S. and Latin American solidarity movements. Resistance to U.S. interventions
and funding to sustain bloody tyrants in the name of anti-communism had grown,
focused on Central America. Local, often faith-based, grassroots movements
against support for death squads in El Salvador and genocidal campaigns
against indigenous peoples in Guatemala, and to provide U.S. sanctuary for
refugees from these conflicts, embraced the Sandinista Revolution as a sign of
hope.

Hundreds of mostly young people joined Nicaragua’s national reconstruction. We
picked coffee and cotton, observed elections and reported on what we saw in a
small nation thrust into the center of international revolutionary
effervescence. _Internacionalistas_ helped in literacy campaigns, built
infrastructure and carried out research that instead of becoming seldom-read
academic papers, formed the basis for new education, development and social
programs.

Dreams die hard, and sometimes it’s difficult to distinguish the moment they
take a turn into nightmare territory. In the mid-nineties, prominent heros of
the revolution began breaking formally with Daniel Ortega, president from
1985-90, then leader of the Sandinista political opposition until returning to
power in 2007. Dora Maria Tellez
[denounced](https://nuso.org/articulo/memorias-de-la-revolucion-y-de-las-
luchas-democratica/) the hijacking of the revolution and started a new
organization in 1995. The Ortegas arrested her in 2021, kept her in solitary
confinement for nearly two years, then expelled her in 2023. The poet-priest,
Ernesto Cardenal, denounced Ortega as authoritarian in 1994 and publicly
opposed him until his passing in 2020. The award-winning writers, Gioconda
Belli and Sergio Ramírez. The list goes on and on.

Nicaraguan feminists and human rights leaders began sounding the alarm decades
ago. The 2006 absolute ban on abortion; rollbacks in women’s rights; the
Ortegas’ denouncement of feminism and misogynist persecution of their own
daughter, Zoilamérica, after she accused her stepfather of sexual abuse;
attacks on [NGOs](https://im-defensoras.org/en/2022/04/international-feminist-
solidarity-in-the-face-of-the-illegal-cancellation-of-womens-rights-supporter-
organizations-or-feminist-organizations-in-nicaragua/) (to date, more than
5,000 have been shut down), the [closing of feminist media](https://im-
defensoras.org/en/2022/08/whrd-alert-nicaragua-daniel-ortega-shuts-down-
feminist-community-radio-station-radio-vos-along-with-eight-other-local-radio-
stations-and-a-television-channel/), and persecution of leading figures left
no room for doubt that the principles of the revolution had been betrayed. The
violent repression of the 2018 pro-democracy uprising in the country that left
some 350 dead ushered in a period of even greater repression. [Constitutional
changes](https://www.oacnudh.org/nicaragua-the-constitutional-reform-deepens-
setbacks-in-civil-and-political-freedoms/) in the constitution in 2025
subordinated all powers to the presidency. With the dismantling of checks and
balances, the presidential couple was clearly laying the foundation for a
perpetual family dynasty.

Ortega’s announcement to cancel elections elicited an immediate response from
the Trump administration. The State Department under Cold War operator-in-
chief and Joe McCarthy’s reincarnation, Marco Rubio, issued a [statement
](https://ni.usembassy.gov/a-call-to-action-addressing-the-murillo-ortega-
dictatorships-vow-to-abolish-elections/)declaring that the announcement ´lays
bare the true authoritarian nature of the Murillo-Ortega dicatatorship´and
warning that Nicaragua “cannot expect to maintain business as usual”. Rubio
[posted](https://x.com/SecRubio/status/2079576369290228200) that “The Trump
Administration and the international community will not stand by as the
Murillo-Ortega dictatorship deepens repression at home and manufactures
instability that threatens U.S. national security.”

So far, no specific measures have been announced. The U.S. government is on
thin ice criticizing anti-democratic measures in the midst of outcry over the
administration’s blatant attempts to fix the electoral system so, in the words
of the president, “the Republicans won’t lose an election for a hundred
years.” Although Nicaragua is theoretically an obstacle in the plan to put the
extreme right in power in all of Latin America, its move toward
authoritarianism, institutionalized patriarchy and neoliberal economics has
placed it closer to the far-right camp than to most leftist leaders.

**María Teresa Blandón: Reflections From Within**

The best way to understand a complex issue is to talk to the people whose
lives are directly affected, the actors on the stage. Days after the
abolishment of elections, I interviewed María Teresa Blandón, Nicaraguan
feminist leader and human rights defender, exiled in Costa Rica since 2022.
Blandón formed part of the Sandinista Front as a rural organizer and cofounder
of the National Farmworkers Association (ATC). The macho violence and the
double day of campesinas working in the field and the home led her to
feminism.

From here, she tells her own story…

**_LC:_**_Were you surprised at Ortega’s announcement?_

**MTB:** Not really, because we had the immediate precedent of the
constitutional reforms illegally passed last year in 2025 that clearly stated
that the people exercise revolutionary power directly through the executive
branch. This constitutional reform revealed the regime’s intention to
terminate the system of elections within a democratic framework.

What probably surprised us is that he said it so directly—they had created the
conditions, we knew they were maneuvering internally to stage an electoral
farse [elections were scheduled for November of this year, a reform extended
the presidential period moving them to 2027, now the proposal is a 7-year term
without open election], but we didn’t expect the audacity of putting it so
explicitly. I think this is what’s caused such a widespread outcry among broad
political sectors in Latin America and the world. It’s a challenge to the
international system to have said it so openly.

**_LC:_**_How will the other branches of government and civil society
respond?_

**MTB:** The precedents go way back, like to 2021 with the electoral farse in
which seven precandidats to the presidency were imprisioned. In 2025, they
took down the pillars of electoral democracy with the constitutional reform
that should have requrired a consitutent assembly because it was practically a
new constitution and that didnt happen. That’s when it became clear that the
powers of the state would be subordinate to the Executive Branch—in fact, the
reform no longer talks about the branches of state power, bur rather of
“organs of the state subordinated to the Executive”.

I really can’t say why the OAS, for example, didn’t activate the Democratic
Charter when the reforms clearly demonstrated that balance of powers and rule
of law no longer existed in Nicaragua. A new totally authoritarian system took
its place that creates the conditions for a dynasty. Now we’re seeing a
reaction because Ortega said it publicly, he summed it up in a single phrase:
“There will be no more elections in Nicaragua”. I think that now some
international actors realize that this is the affirmation of a totalitarian
regime.

**_LC:_**_Do you think that now there will be a response? Would it have an
impact if the OAS activated the Democratic Charter_?

It would have to have an impact for Nicaragua and for the region because if we
accept that a government in Latin America challenges the interamerican system
admitting publicly that it's building a totalitarian regime, then we could
have a perverse effect in the region. Other authoritarian regimes could be
tempted to replicate the Ortega model given that we still don’t see
consequences commensurate to the gravity of the challenge…

The mask is off—there’s no other way to interpret it. The language is
explicit; it is perfectly clear. We are facing a dynastic totalitarian regime
that seeks to remain in power outside the bounds of the law.

**_LC:_**_You were part of Sandinismo with the dream of a new kind of
government and now we see this massive violation of human rights and
democratic principles. How do you respond to those who continue to defend the
regime?_

**MBT:** I think that the Latin American left but also the European left got
thrown off track when Daniel Ortega returned to power in 2007 because they saw
a historic continuity between the revolution and the return of Ortega that
didn’t exist. They were unaware of the conservative alliances that Ortega
forged, even with discredited Liberal Party _caudillos_(strongmen) who had a
serious history of corruption. I think it was easier for them to believe that
there was a leftist, progressive government at the heart of Central America,
but it wasn’t. This Sandinista Front, led by the strongman Daniel Ortega, had
nothing to do with the principles or the hopes that my generation held after
the overthrow of the Somoza dictatorship.

We have been very concerned that this inertia, this silence, has persisted
since 2018. In 2018, it became crystal clear that this was an authoritarian
government capable of using extreme violence to suppress any social protest,
unwilling to respect the rules. So yes, the silence of some leftist
governments has been a heavy blow to social movements and human rights
defenders. By endorsing the Ortega-Murillo regime through their silence, they
aligned themselves with a government that violates human rights, and that
allows the most conservative right-wing rhetoric to stigmatize the left as an
anti-democratic and anti-human rights force…

**_LC:_**_The government has had a particularly problematic relationship with
feminism. Tell us about that and also, this relates to another question: What
were the circumstances behind your departure from the country?_

**MBT:** I’ll start with my story, since that’s the easiest to retell. I was
returning from a conference in Chile and they wouldn’t let me enter Nicaragua
for no reason at all—simply because, at that stage of the repression,
preventing activists, priests and others from entering the country was one of
the main tactics for getting rid of them.

It’s really hard because it forces you to make radical changes in your life
and separate from your family from one minute to another. But I knew that we
feminists had been targeted ever since Ortega’s return to power with his wife.
In 2018, Rosario Murillo issued a manifesto dedicated exclusively to attacking
Nicaraguan feminists. The title referred to “junk feminism”, “false feminism”,
anti-patriotic feminism that serves foreign interests and is atheist. Doña
Rosario said exactly the same thing that far-right conservative groups say.
With the 2018 crisis, feminist organizations were literally dismantled, their
legal status revoked, and their assets confiscated. Since late 2018, no one
has been able to mobilize publicly; social movement activities have been
completely criminalized.

_**LC:** You were separated from your family and your home, but not from your
activism. How do you continue your work from exile? _

**MBT:** Nicaraguan civil society has shown extraordinary commitment with
democratic values and that’s why the Murillo-Ortega regime has not been able
to silence us.We’re spread out in different countries, but we’ve managed to
rebuild our networks to prevent a veil of silence from being cast over
Nicaragua. We’ve continued to document human rights violations and carry out
solidarity campaigns for political prisoners and international advocacy. We
cannot allow a new dynasty to take power in Nicaragua—we already had the
Somoza family for more than 40 years.

_Question from the audience: How widely accepted is the Ortega-Murillo duo
within Nicaragua?_

It’s a good question. Many people on the left thought the regime had strong
popular support, based on Ortega’s claim that he won 82% of the vote in 2021,
but they forgot that the seven opposition candidates were in prison. The
latest reliable independent poll indicates that support for the Ortega-Murillo
regime ranges between 13 and 16%. When you see these big public
demonstrations, it’s because government workers, by executive order, are
required to attend the marches and even forced to bring their families to the
Sandinsta Front marches.

[Ortega’s party] The Sandinista Front is going through its worst period since
2018. It dropped from Ortega’s 40% support in 2006 to no more than 15% today.
The party now operates through fear, with political secretaries exercising
total control over neighborhoods and communities, alongside police and para-
police forces, so people are very afraid—of speaking out, but also of
challenging orders from the secretaries, mayors and security forces. Fear and
necessity carry more weight than support for the leadership.

_**LC:** What final message would you have for the international community?_

**MBT:** The message is that we have a collective responsibility to defend
democracy and human rights. We are living in very dark times, setbacks, marked
by authoritarian leaderships that have become fashionable, so now is the time
for all deocratic forces in the region step forward to defend institutional
frameworks that allow us to live together in safety—not authoritarian safety,
but safety based on democratic consensus.

**What’s next?**

It’s hard to even speculate about how the current political crisis in
Nicaragua will play out. Multilateral diplomatic measures to censure the
Murillo-Ortega regime based on failure to comply with democratic norms could
create needed pressure. Economic sanctions in any form would be a huge
mistake, since they punish a population already suffering.

International solidarity and a determined commitment to democracy and self-
determination brought about the Sandinista Revolution. That’s exactly what it
will take to restore its principles, to build a future where thousands of
Nicaraguans forced into exile, like Maria Teresa Blandón, can return with hope
and confidence and where thousands of Nicaraguans in the country can
participate freely and joyfully in a truly democratic country. This is the
future democratic forces must build together, not just in Nicaragua, but
throughout the Americas.
